newsitem.title: JAPAN: DDI seen returning to group profit in 97/98.
newsitem.headline: DDI seen returning to group profit in 97/98.

text.p: Japanese phone operator DDI Corp will likely see a sharp turnaround in its group profits in the current fiscal year as a huge loss incurred in its PHS handyphone division last year should be substantially cut, analysts say.
They expect DDI to report a relatively strong group net profit forecast for the 1997/98 year ranging from 40 billion to 50 billion yen.
DDI's share price has taken a hit since a Japanese newspaper reported in late April that the company's profit for the current year would likely be 20 billion yen.
The company's forecast figures, along with final results for the 96/97 financial year, which ended on March 31, are to be reported on Thursday.

For the just-completed business year, DDI said in March that it would post a group net loss of 26 billion yen, revising up its earnings forecast as a result of a new agreement with telephone giant NTT Corp lowering fees paid by DDI.
Financial analysts say they expect the final figure to match that estimate and are focussing instead on the prospects for the current year.

"DDI will enjoy rising momentum this year," said Toshiho Sato, analyst at UBS Securities Ltd said. "A smaller loss in the PHS business and a sharp reduction in sales promotion fees will boost the bottom line."
But most analysts said DDI would fail to achieve the target of breaking even in the PHS division, which provides low-cost portable phone service, in the current fiscal year.
They said that high cancellation rates for the lower-tier service and still-expensive access charges paid to NTT for using its local networks would keep the division in the red.
"We believe that a loss-making PHS division in the 1997/98 year could lead to a short-term disappointment in the stock market," said Eric Gan, analyst at Goldman Sachs (Japan) Corp.
Gan said DDI's cancellation rates could rise to 55 percent in 97/98 from an estimated 35 percent in 96/97.

Although other analysts see lower cancellation rates, they agree that the division will rack up losses of about 10 billion yen in 1997/98, down from an estimated 76 billion yen to 77 billion yen loss in 1996/97.
Analysts are also focused on the number of new subscribers for DDI's traditional cellular phone service as costly sales promotion fees paid to handset distributors cut into profits.
"DDI's cellular phone business has gotten out of its worst problems in the first half of 1996/97 and the business will stabilise in 97/98," said Yoshio Ando, analyst at Nomura Research Institute.
